extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutional theorists, and lawmakers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging the legitimacy of conquest, usurpation, tyranny, lawful resistance, and the dissolution of government, as set out in a normative political‑philosophical treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest gives no perpetual title to the conquered people's land
rubrics_metrics.description: No damage men in the state of nature suffer from one another can give a conqueror power to dispossess the posterity of the vanquished or turn them out of their inheritance; the spoil of war (destruction of a few years' produce, plunder of treasure) is not equivalent to the perpetual inheritance of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the relative (imaginary) value of money/treasure versus land; argues that even a just conqueror cannot claim perpetual dominion over the land or posterity of those he has subdued unless legitimate title exists. (See Sect. 184–186, 193–194 for examples and economic comparison.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of a conqueror's rights in (just) war
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conqueror has a just cause, he has a despotical right over the persons of those who actually aided and concurred in the war, and a right to make up his damage and cost out of their labour and estates so far as he injures not the right of any other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits conqueror's authority to those personally implicated in aggression and to compensation for damages; explicitly denies a lawful title to dominion over the whole people or their posterity by virtue of conquest alone. (Sect. 196)

rubrics_metrics.name: Promises and grants extorted by force are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises extorted by force bind not at all; whatever another gets from me by force I still retain the right of, and he is obliged presently to restore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a thief forcing a purse or a pistol at one's breast — such coerced acts do not create legitimate obligations; extorted promises cannot transfer rights because the law of nature obliges only through rightful prescriptions, not through their violation. (Sect. 186)

rubrics_metrics.name: Children of the subdued remain free; conquest does not bind minors
rubrics_metrics.description: The children of those subdued by conquest, being in minority, are freemen; the conqueror's absolute power extends only to the persons actually subdued and dies with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State of parent's subjection cannot forfeit the natural rights of their children; the conqueror cannot lawfully govern children without their own consent. (Sect. 189)

rubrics_metrics.name: Every man has two natural rights: personal liberty and inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is born with a double right: first, a right of freedom to his person; secondly, a right before any other man to inherit with his brethren his father's goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these two rights flows the claim that persons are naturally free from subjection without consent and have property rights in ancestral possessions that cannot be validly taken without consent. (Sect. 190–192)

rubrics_metrics.name: Property granted by a ruler is protected by consent
rubrics_metrics.description: If the conqueror grants estates or possessions to inhabitants, whatever he grants them they have property in, as without a man's own consent property cannot be taken from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples of life grants and inheritances are used to argue that grants create legitimate property rights which arbitrary seizure would violate; otherwise voluntary contracts and grants would be meaningless. (Sect. 193–194)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulers are subject to the laws of God and nature (limits on sovereign exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes owe subjection to the laws of God and nature; grants, promises, and oaths are bonds that hold even the Almighty, and no power can exempt rulers from these obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms moral/legal limits on rulers' behavior; used to rebut claims that sovereigns are above natural law. (Sect. 195)

rubrics_metrics.name: Usurpation is domestic conquest without right
rubrics_metrics.description: Usurpation is getting into the possession of what another has right to; an usurper never has right on his side and cannot be lawfully obeyed because he is not the person the laws have appointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes usurpation (change of persons, not form) from lawful succession; emphasizes that designation of officeholders according to established rules is as necessary as the form of government. Consent of the people is necessary to legitimize anyone who usurps power. (Sect. 197–198)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tyranny defined as exercise of power beyond right for private ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyranny is the exercise of power beyond right, using authority not for the good of those under it but for the ruler's private advantage; when the governor's will is made the rule rather than the law, and actions serve ambition, revenge, or covetousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies equally to monarchies and other forms of government; examples include the Thirty Tyrants, Decemviri. The key evaluative test is whether power is used to preserve people’s properties and the public good. (Sect. 199–201)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful force may be opposed; lawful acts may not
rubrics_metrics.description: Force is to be opposed only to unjust and unlawful force; opposing otherwise draws just condemnation; only hostile force that leaves no remedy of appeal to law justifies violent resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiates cases where immediate self‑defense is necessary (e.g., life threatened on the highway) from cases where legal redress is available (e.g., civil wrongs), which should be pursued by appeal to law. (Sect. 203–207)

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on resisting a prince: sacred person vs illegal acts by agents
rubrics_metrics.description: In some countries the person of the prince is legally sacred and exempt from violence, but illegal acts by his agents (without lawful authority) may be opposed; a commission does not justify acting against the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where the sovereign's person is protected, the law's limits persist: a writ or commission that transgresses legal limits does not authorize unlawful acts. This preserves remedies and prevents unrestricted violence against the sovereign while allowing resistance to illegal exercises of power. (Sect. 205–206)

rubrics_metrics.name: When legal remedy is obstructed, resistance becomes more justified
rubrics_metrics.description: If remedies due by law are obstructed by the power that committed the illegal acts, and appeal to law is not possible, the right of resisting even manifest acts of tyranny becomes more justifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that isolated private resistance is unlikely to overthrow government, but where remedy is blocked and oppression widespread or threatening fundamental rights, resistance may be necessary. (Sect. 207–209)

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad grounds for collective resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If illegal acts extend to the majority of the people, or if oppression threatens all laws, estates, liberties, lives, or religion, the people are morally and practically likely to resist unlawful exercises of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a collective threshold: when oppression appears systemic or threatens the whole community, the justification for resistance grows stronger and widespread action becomes understandable. (Sect. 209)

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptoms and precedents indicating drift toward tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated patterns—arts to elude the law, arbitrary use of prerogative, favouring or suppressing ministers according to aims, experiments of arbitrary power, covertly supporting particular religion—signal a trend toward tyranny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are empirical warning signs that the government is being transformed from lawful rule into arbitrary rule; used as practical indicators for citizens to judge the health of their government. (Sect. 210)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution of society by foreign conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual way a society is dissolved is the inroad of foreign force (conquest) so that the union of the community ceases and individuals return to a state where they may look to other societies for safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When society is dissolved by conquest the government cannot remain; analogy: frame of a house cannot subsist when its materials are scattered. (Sect. 211)

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution from within: alteration or destruction of the legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: When the legislative is broken or dissolved (it being the soul/unifying will of the commonwealth), dissolution and death of the society/government follows because the members no longer have one coherent public will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes the legislative's centrality: the constitution of the legislative is the fundamental act that keeps the community united and able to resolve differences. (Sect. 212)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prince substituting his arbitrary will for the laws alters the legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: If a single person sets up his arbitrary will in place of the laws (the will of the society declared by the legislative), the legislative is effectively changed and the government dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that changing which rules are enforced (not merely persons) constitutes altering the legislative; used to identify when executive overreach has nullified the constitutional order. (Sect. 213–214)

rubrics_metrics.name: Hindering the legislative from assembling or acting is dissolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prince hinders the legislative from assembling in due time or from acting freely, depriving it of the freedom of debating and perfecting what is for the public good, the legislative is altered and the government dissolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on functional capacity (freedom to debate, legislate) rather than identities of members; removing the legislature's working conditions effectively ends its authority. (Sect. 215)

rubrics_metrics.name: Altering electors or methods of election without consent dissolves legislative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prince alters the electors or ways of election without consent and contrary to the common interest, the legislative is altered because those chosen are not the legislative appointed by the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes to the franchise or electoral mechanisms that bypass the people's authorization undermine legitimacy and constitute dissolution from within. (Sect. 216)

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of the people to a foreign power equals change of the legislative
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery of the people into the subjection of a foreign power, whether by prince or legislative, is a change of the legislative and thus a dissolution of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the end of entering society is to be an intact, independent polity governed by its own laws, surrender to foreign rule destroys that purpose and the legislative's authority. (Sect. 217)

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect or abandonment of the executive to execute laws dissolves government
rubrics_metrics.description: When the supreme executive neglects or abandons his charge so that the laws already made can no longer be put in execution, this demonstratively reduces all to anarchy and dissolves the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government without execution of law is equivalent to no government; absence of administration of justice and provision for public necessities shows the government has effectively ceased. (Sect. 219)

rubrics_metrics.name: People retain the right to erect a new legislative when government is dissolved
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved by external or internal means, the people are at liberty to provide for themselves by erecting a new legislative differing in persons or form as they find most for their safety and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms the continuing original right of society to preserve itself and to constitute a new public will; warns against telling people to wait for legal remedy when chains are already on. (Sect. 220)
